One of the biggest mistakes in planted tanks is trying to keep everything too clean. That layer of “gunk” in your substrate and filter? It’s not just waste — it’s part of the ecosystem. Fish poop, decaying leaves, leftover food, and mulm all break down into nutrients your plants actually use. In nature, aquatic plants don’t grow in spotless gravel vacced every week. They grow in nutrient-rich sediment full of decomposing organic matter. A little mulm in the substrate can feed root tabs naturally, support beneficial bacteria, and help heavy root feeders like crypts, swords, and vallisneria thrive. Even biofilm and detritus become food sources for shrimp, snails, and microorganisms that keep the tank balanced. #PlantedTank #Aquascape #AquariumPlants #FishTank #AquariumHobby #FreshwaterAquarium #NatureAquarium #Fishkeeping #Aquascaping #ShrimpTank #LowTechAquarium #AquariumLife

Vacuuming your reef tank sand bed pulls out trapped detritus, keeps phosphate levels stable, and starves nuisance algae before it takes over your saltwater aquarium. But there is a huge catch when doing marine tank maintenance... ⚠️ If you have an established, deep sand bed that has been left untouched for months, do not deep-vacuum it! Plunging a gravel cleaner siphon straight to the bottom can release trapped toxic hydrogen sulphide gas, trigger sharp ammonia spikes, and dump bound nutrients back into the water column, which can easily crash a tank. If your reef substrate is old and undisturbed, stick to light surface siphoning or let a sand-sifting clean-up crew like nassarius snails handle saltwater aquarium cleaning naturally.
